3. The then Bureau of Anti-Corruption investigated the case and submitted a charge sheet on 16-6-2003 against seven accused including the petitioner under sections 409, 420, 467, 468, 471 and 109 of the Penal Code read with section 5(2) of the Act II of 1947 with a sanction of the Government. 

 5. Mr A F Hassan Arif, learned Senior Advocate for the petitioner submits that section 32 of the Durneeti Daman Commission Ain, 2004 (Act V of 2004) mandates no court to take cognizance of an offence scheduled thereto without a sanction accorded by the Anti-Corruption Commission (in brief ACC). The sanction accorded earlier by the Government under section 6(5) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 (Act XL of 1958) does not fulfill the mandatory requirement of section 32 of the Act V of 2004 as it was not accorded by the ACC and, as such, the Senior Metropolitan Special Judge committed gross illegality in taking cognizance of offence against the petitioner without any sanction of the ACC. The proceedings are, therefore, without jurisdiction and liable to be quashed. 

 7. Mr Md Khurshid Alam Khan, learned Advocate for the ACC on the other hand submits that according to the saving clause as provided in section 38(3) of the Act V of 2004, proceeding of an old case will start from where it was at the time of coming in force of the said Act. Since the sanction was already accorded under section 6(5) of the Act XL of 1958, there is no legal requirement of according sanction again by the ACC under section 32 of the Act V of 2004. 

 9. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates of both the sides, examined the record, consulted the relevant provisions of the law and gone through some decisions on the effect of repeal of an Act. It appears that the alleged occurrence took place on 2-2-1991, FIR was lodged on 29-3-1993, investigation was held and charge sheet was submitted on 16-6-2003 by the then Bureau of Anti-Corruption constituted under the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957 (Act XXVI of 1957) with a sanction duly accorded by the Government under section 6(5) of the Act XL of 1958 those were in force at that time. Thereafter, the Act V of 2004 came in force with a provision of sanction to be accorded by the ACC (section 32) and a saving clause (section 38). The Act XXVI of 1957 and the Anti-Corruption (Tribunal) Ordinance, 1960 were repealed by section 38(1) of the Act V of 2004 with effect from establishment of the ACC. Section 6(5) of the Act XL of 1958 was also repealed by Act XXII of 2004 with effect from 12-12-2004 (vide SRO No.330/Law dated 12-12-2004). The new Act i.e. Act V of 2004 in its saving clauses i.e. section 38(3)(4) provides that all incomplete inquiries, investigations under the repealed Act i.e. Act XXVI of 1957, pending proposals for sanctions are to be completed under the new Act and the pending cases in the Tribunals constituted under the repealed Ordinance, 1960 were to be transferred to the Special Judges having territorial jurisdiction over the cases. The saving clauses, however, do not speak of a case where sanction was already accorded under section 6(5) of the Act XL of 1958, but no cognizance was yet taken. The present case falls under this ungiven category, basing which the learned Advocate for the petitioner develops his argument that the provisions of special law are to be followed strictly and non compliance with the same would render the proceedings to be quashed. The learned Advocate, however, does not make any submission on the effect of repeal of an Act in the light of section 6 of the General Clauses Act. 

 10. For better appreciation of the effect of repeal of section 6(5) of the Act XL of 1958 in the present case, let us freshen up our memory by going through the section 6 of the General Clauses Act once again, which runs as under: 

 11. Since no different intention as to the effect on the sanction already accorded by the Government under the repealed law i.e. section 6(5) of the Act XL of 1958 appears in the new Act i.e. Act V of 2004 or in the repealing Act i.e. Act XXII of 2004, it would not affect the sanction accorded under the repealed law. So, the proceedings of the present case shall continue from the stage where the old law i.e. section 6(5) of Act XL of 1958 was repealed. There is nothing in the Act V of 2004 or in Act XXII of 2004 restricting the continuation of the pending proposal for sanction or a sanction already accorded, section 38(3)(4) of the Act V of 2004 rather saves those. 

 12. We also find the case of Tarique Rahman vs Government of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs 63 DLR (AD) 18, wherein the effect of repeal of a law has been dealt with in the following manner: 

 13. In the case in hand, investigation was held under the provisions of the Act XXVI of 1957 and a charge sheet was already submitted by the defunct Bureau of Anti-Corruption on obtaining the sanction under section 6(5) of the Act XL of 1958 those were in force at the relevant time. Thereafter, the proceedings were stayed by the High Court Division and meanwhile the Act V of 2004 came in force with the saving clause as discussed above. Although sub-sections (3)(4) of section 38 of the Act V of 2004 and the Act XXII of 2004 do not specifically deal with the ungiven situation as occurs in the present case, under the facts and circumstances of the case as well as the scheme of the law read with section 6 of the General Clauses Act and the ratio laid down by our Appellate Division in the above cited case of 63 DLR (AD) 18 we are of the view that no new sanction of the ACC is required. The sanction accorded under the repealed section 6(5) of the Act XL of 1958 would suffice. The trial court will start the proceeding from where it was stayed at the time of repealing of section 6(5) of the Act XL of 1958 by Act XXII of 2004. 

 14. In view of the discussions made above, we find no difficulty in holding that the learned Special Judge did not commit any wrong in taking cognizance of offence against the accused in the present case on the basis of the sanction accorded earlier under the repealed law i.e. section 6(5) of the Act XL of 1958. There was no legal requirement of asking for sanction afresh from the ACC under section 32 of the Act V of 2004 read with rule 15 of the Anti-Corruption Commission Rules, 2007. Any fresh sanction would unnecessary delay the trail and defeat the justice, where in the meantime the case has become twenty-three years old. It is against the scheme and purpose of the law as well. We, therefore, do not find any merit in the Rule.
